newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Think-tank sees Hungary GDP growth at 2.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Think-tank sees Hungary GDP growth at 2.5 pct.

text.p: Hungarian independent economic research group Kopint-Datorg said on Tuesday it had upgraded its forecast for the country's 1997 GDP growth to 2.5 percent from 2.0 percent.
"The growth of the Hungarian economy, which started in the second half of last year, has continued and is likely to gather some speed," researcher Gabor Oblath told a news conference.
He added, however, that one pitfall, the exclusive use of the reduction of the forint's crawling peg devaluation as an anti-inflationary tool, needed to be avoided.
"The reduction of inflation can only happen in a coordinated manner by a parallel handling of every factors that affect inflation," Oblath said.
Hungary uses a preannounced crawling peg devaluation system of its currency, with the forint's current monthly devaluation standing at 1.1 percent, to be reduced to 1.0 percent on August 15.

Oblath said that in order to avoid a weakening of the competitiveness of Hungary's exports, a broader agreement was needed than the one which was being negotiated with employers and employees on the size of next year's wage increases.

"There are some backward-looking indexing systems which build past inflation into future prices," Oblath said, adding that these factors increase production costs and could harm firms with a pricing policy based on inflation expectations.
Oblath added that Kopint-Datorg also upgraded its 1997 forecast for the growth of domestic consumption to 1.5 percent from the previous 0.5 percent.

He also said that one basis for GDP growth in 1997 was the pickup of investments, which, contrary to first quarter figures of between three and four percent, was likely to reach 10 percent for the whole year.
"A number of preannounced state investments did not start in the first quarter (of 1997)," Oblath said.
He also said Kopint-Datorg forecast a 12 percent exports growth for 1997 and a 13 percent increase of imports over the same period.
Other Kopint-Datorg forecasts included 18 to 19 percent inflation for 1997 (compared with 23.6 percent in 1996) and a budget deficit of 4.5 to 5 percent of GDP.
Oblath said they expected a current account deficit for the year of around $2 billion and a foreign trade deficit of some $3 billion.
"This means that the foreign trade deficit would remain at a manageable level," Oblath said.
